author: Tara Westover
introFa: کتاب «Educated: A Memoir» نوشته Tara Westover یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Educated: A Memoir»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

Introduction Properties of educated T cells The ability of educated T cells to facilitate the immune response to non-cross-reacting antigens in vitro Thymus-derived cells educated to either keyhole limpet hemocyanin or fowl IgG can reconstitute the response of T cell-depleted spleen cell cultures to other non-cross-reacting antigens. This response can only be obtained if the initial educating antigen is present in culture. The immune response of mouse spleen cells to SRBC as antigen has been extensively studied in vitro. Such work has confirmed much in vivo data relating t o a cooperation between thymus-derived (T cell) and bone mar- row-derived (B cell) lymphocyte to this antigen [ 1-31, The mechanism of this cooperative phenomenon has not yet been ascertained, but the culture situation offers the possibilities for a closer analysis of T cell function. Hartmann [4] and Hunter et al. [5] have described in vitro experiments in which T cells educated to one erythrocyte type could, in the presence of that antigen, facilitate the response of a B cell population to a second erythrocyte anti- gen. There is evidence, however, that the erythrocytes stud- ied in these experiments may cross-react at the T cell level [6]. For this reason, we felt it necessary to pursue these ex- periments further to rule out cross-reactivity as the expla- nation for the phenomenon. We here report that T cells educated to either of 2 protein antigens, KLH and FGG, can, in the presence of these antigens, facilitate the response of B cells to defined ery- throcyte-bound antigens. Some of the properties of this helper function are described. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Animals Mice of the CBA/Ca strain were used. Tissue culture reagents and culture conditions The culture conditions were based largely on those described by Mishell and Dutton [9]. Spleens were removed and gently teased apart in Eagle's minimal essential medium buffered with N-2-hydroxyethylpiperazine-N'-2-ethanesulf0nic acid (HEPES). After suspension with a pasteur pipette, the re- maining tissue fragments were allowed t o settle out at 4 "C. The cells left in suspension were then centrifuged in the cold for 6 min and cell pellets resuspended to concentrations of 0.8 x lo7 - 1 .O x lo7 B cells per ml in culture medium. To this were added varying numbers of educated T cells as re- quired. In most cases, triplicate cultures were performed. RPMI, 1640, fetal bovine serum and concentrates were ob- tained from Flow Laboratories, Irvine, Scotland. Culture medium was prepared by adding non-essential amino acids, glutamine pyruvate and antibiotics with 5 ml fetal bovine serum to 100 ml of RPMI. Nutritional cocktail was prepared and used as described by Dutton [9]. One ml amounts of cell suspensions in culture medium were added to 35 mm Falcon tissue culture dishes with 3 x 1 O6 of either SRBC, DRBC or with 1 x 1 O6 SRBC-TNP as required. The effect of anti-@ treatment The phenomenon we describe as a property of thymus-derived cells is demonstrated in Table 3. In this experiment, the facili- tatory property of the educated T cells was sensitive to anti-@ treatment. but not to anti-Fab treatment. Conversely, our responding B cell populations were relatively insusceptible to the effect of anti-@, but highly sensitive to the anti-Fab in terms of their ability to respond to SRBC. Similar results were obtained using DRBC as antigen for the B cells. Table 5 illustrates the results of an experiment concerned with the specificity of antigen requirement of educated T cells with respect to this facilitatory function. It can be seen that responsiveness can only be obtained in culture if both the educated T cell and its own educating antigen are present together in culture. In other words, the process of passaging thymus cells through an irradiated recipient does not render them susceptible to stimulation by any added protein antigen. It also demonstrates that the phenomenon does not depend upon any nonspecific effect of KLH on T cells. 3.5. Eur. J. Immunol. 1973. 3: 167-172 Properties of educated T cells in vitro 171 It seems unlikely that cross-reaction at the T cell level can explain our data, because we have demonstrated that one can vary the educating antigen and the assay antigens and obtain a similar effect. We have also demonstrated that it is unlikely that the phe- nomenon is dependent o n some recruiting or expanding sub- stance produced by educated T cells which would enable a small number of SRBC-specific T cells to be activated. The simplest explanation would be that educated T cells activated by their specific antigen can release a factor which enhances B cell responsiveness to antigen. Indeed, it has been demonstrated in vitro that allogeneic lymphoid culture supernatants can reconstitute T cell-depleted culture responses to erythrocyte-bound antigens [ 13, 141. Schimpl and Wecker [ 141 consider that there may be two active components in such supernatants, one a “T cell replac- ing factor”, and the second a “T cell expanding factor” which can be observed in cultures only partially depleted of their T cell compartment. It remains to be seen whether such allogeneic factors are at all related to the activity produced by our antigen-triggered, educated T cells. We are at present assaying educated T cell supernatants and looking for soluble factors in double cham- ber cultures using a culture system similar to that described by Feldmann and Basten [IS]. In this system, our preliminary data indicate that there may be a soluble factor which can pass through a 0.4 p nucleopore membrane and facilitate B cell responsiveness. We have, in our experimental system, been able t o select for a non-specific component in a T cell-B cell interaction. How- ever, one should bear in mind that the nonspecific event need not occur at the level of the T cell. For example, if it were the case that activated T cells release an antigen-specific fac- tor, it could be that interaction of this with antigen and an- other cell type or serum factor would generate some non- specific signal. Feldmann and Basten [ 151 provide data which imply the pro- duction of a soluble antigen-specific factor by educated T cells, and they state that they also demonstrate a small nonspecific component. They have studied the responsiveness of hapten- primed B cells and the requirements of such cells may differ from unprimed B cells, which may represent a stage of differ- entiation sensitive to some nonspecific stimulus. We are at present studying the properties of educated T cells in such primed B cell populations to try and explain this discrepancy. There are many observations in the literature which would not restrict the phenomenon we describe to the in vitro situation. In 1916, Weil and Felix [I61 were among the first to describe nonspecific anamestic reactions [ 171. In 1929, Dienes [ 181 demonstrated the development of delayed hypersensitivity to hen ovalbumin injected into a tuberculous lesion. Good [19] and Humphrey and Turk [20] have demonstrated enhanced antibody responses to BGG or diphtheria toxoid when antigen was injected simultaneously with purified pro- tein derivative into animals sensitized to tuberculin. Katz et al. [21] have recently shown that in guinea pigs primed with DNP-ovalbumin, the injection of allogeneic lymphoid cells stimulated synthesis of antibodies to both hapten and carrier in the absence of secondary administration of antigen and heightened the secondary anti-hapten antibody responses to hapten-heterologous carrier conjugates. The first of these phenomena could possibly be explained by released seque- stered antigen occurring during the graft-versus-host reaction, but the latter seems to be similar to that described by Kreth and Williamson [22]. Making use of a hapten-sensitive clone (W I), which they maintain by serial spleen transfers, they demonstrated that the allogeneic stimulus could override the requirement for specific carrier in the clonal response to hapten BGG. C.Y. Wu et al. [23] have described antigenic promotion in rabbits in the hapten antibody response to such antigens as para-azobenzene arsonic acid derivatives of human albumin and of dissociated KLH, in which the promoting ability varied with different macromolecules and seemed to corre- late with the relative magnitude of the carrier effect. Ordal and Grumet* have recently reported that the transfer of parental ( H-2k/k) nonresponder lymphoid cells into he- terologous (H2k/g) nonresponder recipients at the time of primary challenge with (T, G)-A--L elicited the production of both IgM and IgG anti-(T,G)-A--L antibody, even though these strains lack the Ir-1 allele. There are obvious geographical reasons why such a type of effect is not easily observed in vivo. In the restricted micro- environment of a culture vessel there is more likelihood that one may detect active soluble factors which might otherwise be rapidly eliminated in the in vivo situation. With reference to our data, it might be argued that passaging and antigenically stimulating thymus cells in an irradiated recipient in order to produce educated T cells might endow them with properties not available in the unadulterated animal. W e have, however, been able to show similar facilitation of culture responsiveness, sixfold in magnitude, using FGG- primed spleens from a normal donor (unpublished data). This is in agreement with the data of Rubin and Coons [24] using other heterologous antigens. Our data show that it is possible for T cells, stimulated by their specific antigen, to cooperate with B cells, responding to a different antigen. It is not possible to say whether the nonspecific element of this cooperation comes directly from the T cells. Furthermore, it is likely that this is not the only form of cooperation between these cells. This work was supported by grants from the Medical Research Council. We would like to thank Mrs. K. MakelaO determinants Affinity of T and B lymphocyte receptors for hapten Division of Immunobiology, Karolinska I nstitutet, Wallenberglaboratory, Stockholm’, and Department of Serology and Bacteriology, Helsinki University, Helsinkio The affinity of anti-hapten antibodies, produced by single cells, was studied by hapten inhibition of plaque-forming cells using the local hemolysis in gel assay. The shift in affinity of anti-hapten antibodies, that occurs with time after im- munization, was parallelled by an analogous shift, at the cellular level, with re- gard to indirect plaque-forming cells (PFC). Thus, there was a gradual decrease of the hapten concentration which was needed to suppress indirect plaque for- mation with time after immunization, indicating a gradual increase in the num- ber of high affinity cells. No such shift was observed with cells causing direct plaque formation. Analogous studies were performed with hapten-specific antigen-binding cells of T and B origin by using hapten-inhbition of rosette-forming cells. Hapten-spe- cific antigen-binding cells were present in both cell populations. Lymphocyte binding of haptenated red cells could be specifically inhibited by free hapten. It was found that antigen-binding B lymphoid cells became gradually more sus- ceptible to hapten inhibition with time after immunization, whereas no such change was observed in antigen-binding T lymphoid cells. Possible reasons for this discrepancy are discussed, as well as the implications for these findings re- garding the specificity and structure of the T cell receptors. 1.
